source.title: MAxBench: A Multinomial Concept Recovery Benchmark
source.authors: Divya Appapogu; Freya Behrens; Yonatan Belinkov; Aaron Mueller

record.tranche_reason: The study uses DiffMean-r1 as a one-direction localization baseline and reports its concept-steering scores, but does not test refusal or any of the claim's other specified behaviors.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates steering for multinomial semantic concepts, not harmful-request refusal, refusal ablation or addition, abliteration, jailbreaks, harmfulness judgments, transfer of a refusal direction, or reasoning models. Its DiffMean-r1 results are recorded as related but not version-specific findings. Other cited results are not included.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks localization methods for multinomial semantic concepts (ANIMALS, DAYS, etc.) and cites Arditi et al. only as an example that binary concepts like refusal need one direction. It never measures refusal, harmful-request behaviour, ablation, abliteration, jailbreaks or reasoning models. DiffMean-r1 appears as a generic concept-steering baseline, not as the refusal direction, so this is citation plus unrelated use of the same estimator (T6, not T4).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that affine subspaces recover multinomial concepts more reliably than rank-one or linear subspaces, largely due to non-zero offsets. Manifold steering is competitive where applicable. No method consistently beats prompting when models are capable enough. Refusal is only mentioned as a binary concept where one direction suffices (citing Arditi et al.).
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a difference-in-means rank-one baseline for non-refusal concepts, then steers by sampling and interpolating activations; it does not apply the refusal-direction ablation/addition tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported steering performance varies across models and concept settings; the study also varies representation rank and reports differences between complete and incomplete DAYS spline data.

fits_no_version.finding: For multinomial semantic concepts, rank-one DiffMean-r1 steering scores lower than affine multidimensional methods across four instruction-tuned models. Much of the gap comes from a non-zero offset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multinomial (non-binary) concepts are better captured by affine subspaces than by a single difference-in-means direction. The paper itself frames refusal as the binary case where one direction suffices.

record.problems: The study states that most experiments rely on LLM judges, which may disagree with human judgments; it evaluates only a single intervention layer and requires hyperparameter tuning for sampling and steering.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-related rows retained. Results for other localization methods and other concepts are not outcomes of the claim's refusal mechanism.

untested.parts: All: no refusal direction is extracted, ablated or added.
All for refusal. Multidimensionality is shown only for semantic concepts.
All: no harmfulness or refusal representations.
All: no transfer of a refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6. The study does not use the refusal direction as a tool. It uses the generic difference-in-means estimator on unrelated concepts. Its V4-like multidimensionality finding concerns semantic concepts, not refusal, so it is not linked to V4.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal direction discovery, removal and addition; refusal behavior; preservation of general capability under refusal ablation.
Weight-edit ablation and refusal in released models.
Jailbreak suppression of the refusal direction and robustness training against its ablation.
Whether refusal is represented by an affine space, cone, or multiple directions.
Separate encoding of harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Effects of refusal-training method or timing on the existence of a removable direction.
